verses.translation_literal: And the famine [was] heavy in the land.
verses.translation_dramatic: And still the famine pressed on the land, heavy as a hand laid on the back of the neck. The sky gave nothing, the fields gave nothing, and the weight did not lift.
verses.directors_commentary:
No new scene begins here, only a weight that never left. Hebrew says the famine was *kaved*, 'heavy', the same root that elsewhere means honor, glory and a stubborn heart (Pharaoh's heart is *kaved* in Exodus). The KJV's 'sore' is archaic for 'grievous' and loses the physical image of weight; modern 'severe' loses it too. Play it as a load the whole company is carrying.

The verse is also a hinge. Chapter 42 ended with Jacob refusing to let Benjamin go; the narrator now lets hunger do what argument could not. Radak, reading verse 43:1 beside verse 2, hears Judah telling his brothers to wait until the house's grain is finished, so that the old man will consent: the famine is the pressure working on Jacob.

philological_notes.note: 'Heavy'. The same root gives 'glory' (*kavod*) and is used of a hardened heart. The famine is a weight, not just a shortage. KJV 'sore' blurs this.

verses.translation_literal: And it was when they finished to eat the grain which they had brought from Egypt, and their father said to them, Return, buy for us a little of food.
verses.translation_dramatic: The last of the Egyptian grain went into the pot, and then the sacks were empty and the house was quiet in the wrong way. It was their father who broke the silence, and he did not say Benjamin's name. 'Go back,' said Jacob. 'Buy us a little food.'
verses.directors_commentary:
Jacob speaks first, and that is the surprise. Judah's whole speech that follows is a reply to a father who has not mentioned Benjamin at all. Jacob says 'a little food', and the word is *me'at*, 'a small amount': he is bargaining even with starvation, hoping a small errand will spare him the real one. Play Jacob as a man who has done the arithmetic and is trying to avoid its answer. Sforno hears more: Jacob suspects the sons want to take Benjamin to be rid of him, as Joseph was lost (he cites 42:36).

The KJV 'eaten up the corn' is correct for its day but 'corn' is a trap: in English usage of 1611 it means any grain, here wheat or barley, not maize. 'Their father said' in the KJV also smooths a Hebrew that begins with the clumsy, spoken-sounding 'and it was when… and he said', a narrator's stumble that lets the scene begin mid-breath. Rashi notes that *kalu* here means the food was all gone (Aramaic *shetsi'u*), not merely 'enough' as in Genesis 24:19.

philological_notes.note: 'Buy grain'. The root *shavar* means both 'break' and 'buy grain': grain is 'broken' from the stores. Egypt is the source, so the verb of buying is the same word that runs through chapters 41–47.
'They finished'. Rashi distinguishes this 'ended entirely' from the Aramaic *safiku* ('sufficed') used by Onkelos, and says the grain was truly gone.

verses.translation_literal: And Judah said to him, saying, Warning he warned against us, the man, saying, You shall not see my face, unless your brother [is] with you.
verses.translation_dramatic: Judah answered, and his voice was level, the voice of a man who has rehearsed this a hundred times in his head. 'The man warned us. He warned us, and he meant it. You will not see my face, he said, unless your brother is with you.'
verses.directors_commentary:
Judah has quietly taken the lead from Reuben, who offered his two sons as a pledge in 42:37 and was ignored. Judah does not argue emotion; he argues law. *Ha'ed he'id* is the emphatic doubled form, the language of a formal warning given before witnesses. Rashi and Radak both say exactly this: a *hatra'ah*, the warning that must precede any penalty. Judah is telling his father that this is not a mood of the Egyptian governor but a stated condition with consequences.

The KJV 'did solemnly protest' captures the doubling well. What it hides is 'my face': the Hebrew *panai* is the formal idiom for an audience with a ruler. To 'see the face' of a great man is to be admitted into his presence, and to be denied it is to be denied the grain. Note that Judah, quoting the Egyptian, says 'the man' and not 'the lord of the land' as the brothers called him earlier: he speaks of him almost as a threat that has no name.

philological_notes.note: Infinitive absolute with finite verb: 'warned emphatically'. Rashi and Radak explain it as a legal warning given before witnesses (*hatra'ah*).
'My face': an audience with an official. To 'see the face' is to be received.

verses.translation_literal: If there is you sending our brother with us, we will go down and we will buy for you food.
verses.translation_dramatic: 'If you will send our brother with us,' said Judah, 'we will go down, and we will buy you food.'
verses.directors_commentary:
Judah makes the offer in terms of Jacob's own need: 'buy *for you* food'. Not for us, not for the children, but for the old man whose consent is required. The Hebrew uses *yesh*, 'there is', with a suffix, 'if there is you sending', an idiom for 'if you are willing and able', the way English says 'if you are prepared to'. KJV 'if thou wilt send' gets this right but flattens the formality.

'Go down' is geography and not just direction: Egypt is downhill from the hill-country of Hebron, and Genesis always speaks of 'going down' to Egypt, a verb that carries the weight of leaving the Promised Land. Jacob will feel it.

philological_notes.note: *Yesh* ('there is') with a pronoun suffix, followed by a participle: 'if you are [prepared to be] sending'. A polite, conditional idiom.

verses.translation_literal: And if there is not you sending, we will not go down, for the man said to us, You shall not see my face, unless your brother [is] with you.
verses.translation_dramatic: 'But if you will not send him, we will not go down. We cannot. The man said it plainly: you will not see my face unless your brother is with you.'
verses.directors_commentary:
The second half of the ultimatum is the mirror of the first, and Judah repeats the Egyptian's words nearly verbatim from verse 3: a negotiator who will not paraphrase. Note that 'we will not go down' is the first time any of the sons has refused their father outright. It is respectful but absolute.

The KJV adds 'him' in italic-style ('wilt not send him'), which is not in the Hebrew: the object is simply understood, and the omission matters because Judah leaves Benjamin unnamed. In the whole exchange no one in this scene says 'Benjamin'. He is 'the brother', 'the boy', 'him': a presence in the room that everyone is stepping around.

verses.translation_literal: And Israel said, Why did you do evil to me, to tell the man whether you still [have] a brother?
verses.translation_dramatic: 'Why?' The old man's voice cracked on the word. 'Why did you do this evil to me? Why did you tell the man that you had another brother?'
verses.directors_commentary:
The narrator switches the name: Jacob becomes *Israel*, the name given at the Jabbok after wrestling. In this book, the name appears when Jacob speaks as patriarch and as one of those who struggle with God and men. Here he does both, as a father and as the head of a clan at the edge of ruin. Play him as someone who is not angry so much as wounded; the accusation 'you did evil to me' is a cry, not a charge.

The verb *hare'otem* is the causative of the root *r-'-'* ('to be bad'): 'you made it bad for me', 'you caused me harm'. The KJV 'dealt ye so ill with me' is acceptable, but 'ill' sounds like manners; Israel is saying they hurt him. The BBE 'cruel' puts the force back. Ironically the brothers had little choice; verse 7 is their answer.

philological_notes.note: Causative (hiphil) of *ra'a'*: 'to do harm to, to make bad for'. Stronger than KJV 'dealt ill'.

verses.translation_literal: And they said, Asking he asked, the man, about us and about our kindred, saying, Is your father still alive? Is there to you a brother? And we told him on the mouth of these words. Knowing, could we know that he would say, Bring down your brother?
verses.translation_dramatic: 'He questioned us,' they said. 'The man questioned us closely, about ourselves, about our family. Is your father still living? Do you have another brother? We only answered what he asked. How could we have known he would say, Bring your brother down?'
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the brothers' defense, and it is the most human speech in the scene: a group of men, all talking at once, explaining that none of it was their fault. *Sha'ol sha'al* is again the emphatic doubling, 'he asked and asked': he interrogated them. The Egyptian's questions about father and family, in the brothers' report, sound like a polite stranger; to Jacob they must sound like a trap, and to the reader who knows who the Egyptian is they are the questions of a brother starving for news. The irony is the point.

KJV 'asked us straitly' preserves the sense but 'straitly' is obsolete for 'strictly, closely'. 'According to the tenor of these words' renders *'al pi*, literally 'upon the mouth of', that is, 'according to what his questions required'. Rashi: they were compelled to answer by his questions. Rashi also has the midrashic touch that he asked even about the 'wood of our cradles', which shows how thorough the interrogation felt to those who remembered it.

The closing rhetorical question uses the doubled infinitive again, *hayado'a neda'*: 'could we really have known?' It is the cry of every witness who answered honestly and was punished for it.

philological_notes.note: Infinitive absolute plus finite verb: 'he asked and asked', 'questioned closely'. Rashi's midrash: even the 'wood of our cradles' was revealed.
'Our kindred, our birth-family'. From the root 'to bear', it covers the extended family into which one is born.
Literally 'on the mouth of'. Idiom: 'according to, as dictated by'. The questions set the terms of the answers.

verses.translation_literal: And Judah said to Israel his father, Send the young man with me, and let us rise and go, and we shall live and not die, both we, both you, both our little ones.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then Judah turned to his father and spoke the words that cost him everything. 'Send the boy with me. Let us rise and go, and we will live, and we will not die: we, and you, and our little ones.'
verses.directors_commentary:
Judah's plea builds like a litany. *Qum* and *lekh*, 'rise and go', are the language of decision: the same pair of verbs that begins Abraham's journey. And 'live and not die' echoes Joseph's own words in 42:18–20, 'do this and live'; Sforno hears in 'not die' the Egyptian's promise to them. The triple *gam*, 'both we, as well as you, as well as our little ones', counts the household in widening circles until the smallest children are in the room. He does not mention Benjamin's danger; he speaks of the deaths on the other side of the balance. Radak and Rashi read it as the argument of the certain against the uncertain: a possible loss against a certain famine.

The KJV 'lad' and 'little ones' are fair. The Hebrew *na'ar* is a young man, Benjamin being by now in his twenties; Jacob's refusal to see him as anything but a child is part of the scene. Rashi's remark that Judah was moved by the holy spirit is a rabbinic touch: 'that we may live' foretells that Jacob's spirit will revive (45:27).

philological_notes.note: 'The young man, the lad'. Not necessarily a child; Benjamin is of age, though his father treats him as a boy.
'Our little ones', the dependent children, a collective for those who cannot travel or fend for themselves.
Repeated *gam* piles up the household one group at a time; Ibn Ezra and Radak note this as the idiom of the holy tongue.

verses.translation_literal: I, I will be surety for him; from my hand you shall seek him. If I do not bring him to you and set him before you, then I will have sinned to you all the days.
verses.translation_dramatic: 'I will be his surety,' said Judah. 'Take him from my hand. If I do not bring him back to you, if I do not stand him in front of you, then let the guilt be mine, all my days.'
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the pledge on which the rest of the book turns. Judah is the man who proposed selling Joseph (37:26–27) and who now stakes his life on keeping the other son of Rachel safe. *'Arav* is the commercial verb of suretyship: the guarantor puts himself in the debtor's place. The forms are legal: 'from my hand you shall seek him' is the formula for a guarantor's liability (compare 31:39, where Jacob tells Laban that he made good every loss 'from my hand'). The pronoun *anokhi* stands first, emphatic: 'I myself'. Reuben had offered his sons, a gesture; Judah offers himself.

The KJV 'bear the blame for ever' is a good paraphrase, but the Hebrew is blunter: *hatati lekha*, 'I will have sinned against you'. The word is the one for offense, culpability before a person who can demand an account. Rashi takes 'all the days' to mean the world to come: the pledge is eternal. Radak draws the rabbinic rule that a conditional ban binds even on oneself, and adds a legend (Makkot 11b) that Judah's bones rolled in his coffin through the desert for this oath until Moses prayed for him (Deuteronomy 33:7). Treat these as the tradition's reading of how seriously the oath was taken.

philological_notes.note: 'I will be surety for him': the commercial verb of guaranteeing a debt or person. Judah uses it again in 44:32. Related to the noun *'eravon*, pledge.
'I will have sinned', 'I will be culpable': a perfect with a conditional sense. The offense is against the father, not only before God.

verses.translation_literal: For if we had not delayed, for now we would have returned these two times.
verses.translation_dramatic: 'For if we had not lingered,' Judah said, and his voice went hard, 'we could have been there and back twice by now.'
verses.directors_commentary:
A bitter little verse. The pressure of Judah's voice should be heard: every day of this argument was a day of hunger. *Hitmahmah* is a stuttering, reduplicated verb, from the root *m-h-h*, 'to linger, to hesitate', and the sound of the word itself dawdles. The KJV 'except we had lingered, surely now we had returned this second time' is archaic and the 'this second time' is wrong: the Hebrew *zeh pa'amayim* means 'these two times', that is, 'twice already'. The BBE gets nearer the sense. Rashi hears an accusation: had you not delayed, we would have come back with Simeon and you would not have grieved all these days. Simeon is still in an Egyptian prison, a fact Judah does not name.

Note how Judah's diplomacy has a sharp edge: after the pledge, the reproach. The old man hesitates; his sons have been waiting.

philological_notes.note: 'We lingered, dawdled'. A reduplicated reflexive form whose stuttering shape mimics hesitation.
'These two times', that is, twice. KJV 'this second time' misreads the dual.

verses.translation_literal: And Israel their father said to them, If so, then, this do: take from the song-of the land in your vessels, and take down to the man a gift: a little balm and a little honey, gum and ladanum, pistachios and almonds.
verses.translation_dramatic: And Israel was silent a long while. Then he spoke, and his voice was a father's, practical, bleak and spent. 'If it must be so, then do this. Take the best the land sings of, in your vessels, and carry it down to the man as a gift: a little balm, a little honey, gum and myrrh, pistachios and almonds.'
verses.directors_commentary:
Jacob yields, and the way he yields is revealing. He does not say yes to Benjamin; he says *'im ken efo*, 'if it is so, then', a phrase soaked in resignation. Rashi hears a man who has to find the cure for his own decision. He surrenders to necessity and begins to plan, which is what practical fathers do.

The gift is a diplomatic present, a *minchah*, the same word later used for grain offerings and tribute. Jacob has done this before: Sforno notes that his gift to Esau (ch. 32–33) was large to please a covetous eye, while this one is small, choice and rare, fit for a wealthy man who counts nothing. These are the goods Canaan exported: Radak cites Ezekiel 27:17 for balm and honey in the trade of Judah and Israel with Tyre. Balm, gum and ladanum were aromatics and cosmetics, honey (probably fruit syrup, perhaps of grapes) a luxury, pistachios and almonds foods that Egypt did not grow in quantity.

The phrase *mizimrat ha'aretz*, 'from the *zimrah* of the land', is a famous puzzle. The word is built on the root of 'song' (*zemer*): 'what the land is praised for', 'what it sings about'. Rashi's reading, 'that which everyone sings about when it comes into the world', and Ibn Ezra's 'anything excellent' agree. The KJV 'best fruits' is a decent guess, but it drops the music. The botanical terms are uncertain: Rashi admits he does not know *botnim*, Radak says pine nuts, Ibn Ezra 'walnuts, some say'; *nekhot* is gum tragacanth or storax, *lot* ladanum or mastic (Radak, citing Genesis Rabbah). KJV 'spices and myrrh' is traditional; 'balm' for *tsori* is the conventional rendering of an unidentified resin.

philological_notes.note: A hapax built on the root of 'song' or 'praise': 'what the land is praised for', its choice products. Rashi and Ibn Ezra read it as the most renowned products; KJV 'best fruits'.
A gift, tribute or present offered to a superior, to win favour. Later also the grain offering.
'Balm', a resin exported from Gilead (compare Ezekiel 27:17). The plant is unidentified.
Probably pistachios. Rashi says he does not know what they are; Radak identifies them as pine nuts; Ibn Ezra says some say walnuts.
'Then, in that case': a particle of resignation. Rashi reads it as Jacob reasoning himself into the necessary arrangement.

verses.translation_literal: And silver, double, take in your hand, and the silver that was returned in the mouth of your sacks, take back in your hand; perhaps it [was] a mistake.
verses.translation_dramatic: 'And take silver, twice the sum, in your hands. The silver that was put back in the mouths of your sacks, carry that back too, with your own hands. Perhaps it was a mistake.'
verses.directors_commentary:
Jacob turns a practical eye on the one thing that frightened him in chapter 42: money that came back unasked. His reading, 'perhaps a mistake', is hopeful and a little naive; the reader knows it was planted. *Mishgeh* is an error made without intent, the oversight of a careless clerk. KJV 'peradventure it was an oversight' is accurate; 'peradventure' for *ulai* is merely archaic for 'perhaps'.

The repeated 'in your hand' is the whole point. Silver was weighed, not counted coins, and carried in the hand to show that nothing was hidden: you do not smuggle back what you plan to confess. *Kesef mishneh* is either 'double the silver' (Rashi: twice the first sum) or 'a second sum' for the new purchase over and above the returned money (Radak reads it as 'second silver', comparing Jeremiah 17:18). The ambiguity is real. The sense is the same: take enough to pay for the old grain and the new. Rashi adds a market prudence: the price may have risen. Radak guesses that the sellers' own silver bundles had slipped into the measure with the grain, and that returning it would make the brothers look honest.

philological_notes.note: 'Double silver' or 'a second sum of silver'. Rashi: twice the original amount; Radak: a second silver, as in Jeremiah 17:18.
An unintended error or oversight. Rashi proposes that the steward forgot to take it; Rashbam that it was left as a marker to identify each sack.

verses.translation_literal: And [obj] your brother, take, and arise, return to the man.
verses.translation_dramatic: And your brother, take him too. Get up now, and go back to the man.
verses.directors_commentary:
Israel's voice here is a string of bare commands: take, arise, return. No 'please', no argument. A father who has lost every argument gives orders because he has no more reasons. The word order puts 'your brother' first, before the verbs: the one thing he cannot say aloud is the name Benjamin.

The KJV's 'take also your brother' adds 'also' and smooths the staccato; 'go again' is archaic for 'return'. Note 'the man': the brothers and their father never call Joseph anything else. Only the reader knows who he is.

philological_notes.note: Two imperatives side by side, 'arise, return': a pair of verbs that makes the order urgent, not two separate actions. The KJV 'arise, go again' keeps the pair but the sense of 'return' (shuv) is lost in 'go again', and shuv will recur through the chapter as the key verb for money, men and the sons coming back.

verses.translation_literal: And El Shaddai, may he give to you compassion before the man, and he will send to you [obj] your brother, another, and [obj] Benjamin. And I, as I have been bereaved, I have been bereaved.
verses.translation_dramatic: And may God Almighty give you mercy in that man's eyes. May he let your other brother go, and Benjamin with him. As for me, if I must be bereaved, then I am bereaved.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is a blessing and a surrender in one breath. 'May El Shaddai give you rachamim' is the only place in the chapter where Jacob names God, and he does so for the one power the sons need and he lacks: the word rachamim is 'womb-feelings', the tenderness of a mother for her child. He prays that a stranger will feel for them what a parent feels, and the stranger is, unknown to him, his own son. Play the line quietly; Jacob does not know the irony.

The KJV 'send away' blurs shillach, which in a prisoner context means 'release' (Radak reads it as freeing him from custody). 'Your other brother' is Simeon in Rashi's reading, but the Hebrew only says 'another one', and Ramban and Genesis Rabbah note that Jacob may also mean Joseph in a half-prayer. Notice he cannot even say Simeon's name.

The last clause is a fixed form: 'as I have been bereaved, I have been bereaved', with the same verb twice (shakol). The KJV adds 'of my children', which is not in the Hebrew; the verb stands bare, as a shrug of grief. Rashbam and Ramban compare Esther 4:16, 'if I perish, I perish': the speaker has nothing left to lose. Say it flat, not weeping.

philological_notes.note: The patriarchal divine title El Shaddai, 'God Almighty' in tradition. Rashi gives a pun on 'sufficient' (dai): the God who said 'enough' to the world will say 'enough' to my troubles. This is his midrashic reading, not a settled etymology.
'Compassion', from the same root as rechem, womb; the plural expresses deep, parental feeling. KJV 'mercy' is acceptable but loses the family tone.
The verb repeated, the first with a vowel pattern of a state and the second of an act (Radak). Ramban reads it as 'you cannot add to my bereavement: I am already bereaved'. Parallel: Esther 4:16.

verses.translation_literal: And the men took [obj] this gift, and double silver they took in their hand, and [obj] Benjamin; and they arose and went down [to] Egypt and stood before Joseph.
verses.translation_dramatic: So the men took up the gift, and silver twice over in their hands, and Benjamin. They rose, they went down into Egypt, and they stood before Joseph.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verbs march: took, took, took, arose, went down, stood. The text lists Benjamin between the silver and the gift, as one more thing to be carried. That is how the brothers have been made to treat him by their father's fear. The chain ends with 'stood before Joseph', the same verb of standing that echoes the dreams in which they were to bow. They stand; the bowing comes later.

The KJV 'that present' is fine. But 'double money' sounds like interest: it is mishneh kesef, a second portion of silver, the original sum plus what they found, per verse 12. 'Went down' is literal: Egypt is downhill from Canaan, and 'going down' is the book's standing phrase for the journey.

The Targum and Rashi note that Aramaic uses different verbs for taking silver in the hand and for taking a person: Benjamin is 'led', not 'taken'.

philological_notes.note: 'A double of silver', that is, twice the sum, not interest. Compare the instruction in 43:12.
The same verb 'took' governs Benjamin. Rashi notes that Onkelos renders the taking of Benjamin with a verb of leading, because Aramaic distinguishes taking an object from leading a person.

verses.translation_literal: And Joseph saw Benjamin with them, and said to [the one who was] over his house: Bring [obj] the men to the house, and slaughter a slaughter, and prepare, for with me the men will eat at noon.
verses.translation_dramatic: Joseph looked, and Benjamin was among them. He turned to the man over his house. 'Bring these men into my house. Slaughter, and make it ready, for they will eat with me at noon.'
verses.directors_commentary:
Joseph sees Benjamin, and the text gives us only the seeing. Give the actor a beat of silence; everything he feels is held in the verb. Then his voice becomes administrative: bring, slaughter, prepare. The emotion goes underground into a household order.

He says 'slaughter a slaughter' (tevach tevach): an infinitive absolute with its verb, which means a real slaughter of an animal, a feast, not a snack. Rashi notes the form is odd as a command. The KJV 'slay' sounds like killing men; the Hebrew is ritual and kitchen slaughter. Meat was for festivals and honored guests, so this signals status. The KJV 'ruler of his house' and 'dine' are acceptable; 'steward' (ASV) captures the office, literally 'the one over his house'.

Tsohorayim is 'noon' (the dual: the double light of midday). Radak says it was when the great and the judges ate, after the morning's work; Sforno suggests Joseph was at the king's gate. A meal at his table means these foreign shepherds are being treated as equals, which should terrify them.

philological_notes.note: Imperative with an absolute infinitive and its noun: 'slaughter a slaughter'. Rashi observes the form reads like 'to slaughter a slaughter', and that the imperative would normally be tevach.
'At noon', a dual form for the two lights of midday. Radak ties it to the hour of the rulers' meal (Ecclesiastes 10:16).

verses.translation_literal: And the man did as Joseph said, and the man brought [obj] the men [to] the house of Joseph.
verses.translation_dramatic: The man did exactly as Joseph had said. He led the men toward the house of Joseph.
verses.directors_commentary:
A verse of pure obedience, with 'the man' repeated twice and 'Joseph' twice, as if a ledger entry. There is no emotion, only the machinery of the household starting up, which is why the next verse lands so hard: the brothers hear this as a trap.

The KJV 'bade' is archaic for 'said'; the Hebrew is the plain verb 'said'. Note the directional ending in beitah: 'toward the house', a movement, not yet inside.

verses.translation_literal: And the men were afraid because they were brought [to] the house of Joseph, and they said: On account of the silver that was returned in our sacks at the beginning we are being brought, to roll himself upon us and to throw himself upon us, and to take us for slaves, and [obj] our donkeys.
verses.translation_dramatic: And fear took the men, because they were being led into Joseph's house. They whispered it to one another: 'It is the silver. The silver that was put back in our sacks the first time. That is why we are brought here, so that he can fall on us, and seize us as slaves, and our donkeys too.'
verses.directors_commentary:
The brothers have just been honored, and they read it as a snare. This is guilt reading signs: a guest who is never a guest is a prisoner. Ancient travelers going to buy grain slept in the town's inns, not in the vizier's house (Rashi), so the invitation itself looks wrong to them. Play it as a whisper among men who have been on edge for months.

Two rare verbs carry the dread: lehitgolel and lehitnappel, 'to roll himself upon us' and 'to throw himself upon us'. Both are reflexive: he will do it of his own accord, as a man hurls himself on someone. Rashi and Ramban read the first as a charge 'rolling' onto them, and Onkelos as a pretext. The KJV has 'seek occasion against us, and fall upon us', which softens the physical image into a legal one. In the Hebrew they feel a body coming down on them.

The last words are the ones that give them away: 'and our donkeys', the pack animals that carry the family's life home. Ramban says they fear the grain cannot be sent home and all will starve. 'Slaves' is plain 'avadim'; KJV's 'bondmen' is archaic.

philological_notes.note: Reflexive 'to roll oneself upon': a charge or accusation rolling down on them (Rashi), or a man tumbling over his fellow (Ramban, citing 2 Samuel 20:12).
Reflexive 'to throw oneself upon', a deliberate attack with one's full height (Ramban).
'At the beginning', that is, on the first journey; also in 43:20. KJV 'at the first time' is awkward.

verses.translation_literal: And they drew near to the man who was over the house of Joseph, and they spoke to him [at] the entrance of the house.
verses.translation_dramatic: They drew close to the man who was over Joseph's house, and there, at the threshold, before they dared to step inside, they spoke to him.
verses.directors_commentary:
They stop at the door. Rashbam says they spoke before entering; Radak adds a motive, so that the household would not overhear. A man who is afraid wants to settle his debt on the doorstep, with a witness at hand and the street behind him. Stage this with the brothers clustered tight, the steward blocking the way in.

The verb vayigeshu, 'drew near', is the same one Judah will use in 44:18 when he approaches Joseph himself. The KJV 'communed' is archaic for 'spoke' and now sounds devotional. 'The man who was over the house' is the steward, an office with real authority.

philological_notes.note: 'The opening of the house': they speak before crossing it, which Rashbam and Radak both take as deliberate.

verses.translation_literal: And they said: Pardon, my lord! Coming down, we came down at the beginning to buy food.
verses.translation_dramatic: 'Please, my lord,' they said. 'We did come down once before. We came down for one thing only: to buy food.'
verses.directors_commentary:
The speech begins with a cry: bi adoni. It is a petition, two words that sound like a man dropping to his knees. The sources disagree on what exactly it is. Rashi takes it from an Aramaic word of plea; Ramban rejects that and says it is a cry of protest at injustice; Ibn Ezra reads a short form of 'on me, my lord, be the guilt' (1 Samuel 25:24). All agree the tone is begging. The KJV 'O sir' reduces it to a polite address.

Then 'yarod yaradnu', 'coming down, we came down', the verb doubled for emphasis: we really did come down. The KJV 'we came indeed down' keeps this. Rashi also hears a social note in 'down': we, who were used to feeding others, now need you. The brothers insist on their one innocent purpose, food.

philological_notes.note: A plea formula, 'pardon, my lord'. Rashi derives it from an Aramaic word for request; Ramban disputes that and calls it a cry of distress; Ibn Ezra reads it as an abbreviated 'upon me, my lord, [be the guilt]'. The meaning of a petition is shared by all.
Infinitive absolute and finite verb: 'we truly came down'. Rashi adds that going down is also a decline in status for them.

verses.translation_literal: And it was, when we came to the lodging place, and we opened our sacks, and behold: the silver of each man in the mouth of his sack, our silver in its weight; and we have brought it back in our hand.
verses.translation_dramatic: At the place where we stopped for the night, we opened our sacks, and there it was. Each man's silver lay in the mouth of his sack, our own silver, every shekel of its weight. And here we have brought it back in our hands.
verses.directors_commentary:
The brothers tell the story in the order it happened, as men who have rehearsed it on the road. The word 'behold' (hinneh) puts the audience inside the moment of finding. They stress 'in its weight': nothing was missing, nothing was added, so no one can say they cheated. In a world where silver was weighed on scales, not counted as coins, the exact weight is proof of honesty. Sforno adds that it was the very same pieces, which is why they did not think it a mistake from another's payment.

The KJV 'inn' is misleading: a malon is a night stopping-place, perhaps no more than a campsite with a well. 'The mouth of his sack' is literal; ancient sacks were tied at the neck.

philological_notes.note: 'In its weight': silver was paid by weight. Sforno reads that it was the same coins, which is why they thought no mistake had been made.
A night-stop, from lun 'to lodge'. KJV 'inn' suggests a building with a keeper.

verses.translation_literal: And other silver we have brought down in our hand to buy food. We do not know who put our silver in our sacks.
verses.translation_dramatic: And we have brought other silver down with us, to buy food. As for the first silver, we do not know who put it in our sacks.
verses.directors_commentary:
The brothers close their case with two things: restitution and ignorance. 'Other silver' is a second sum, fresh money for the new purchase, separate from the returned money, which they have brought back. Then the declaration: 'we do not know who put it'. This is true, but it is not the whole truth: they suspect God's hand, as they said in 42:28. They are careful here to say nothing a steward could take as an accusation.

The KJV 'we cannot tell' is a Briticism for 'we do not know'; the Hebrew is the flat 'do not know'. The question word 'who' (mi) opens the unanswered riddle that Joseph's steward will answer in the next verse, with a pious non-answer.

verses.translation_literal: And he said: Peace to you, do not fear. Your God and the God of your father gave you treasure in your sacks. Your silver came to me. And he brought out to them [obj] Simeon.
verses.translation_dramatic: 'Peace to you,' he said. 'Do not be afraid. Your God, the God of your father, put a hidden treasure into your sacks. Your silver reached me.' And then he brought Simeon out to them.
verses.directors_commentary:
The steward's first word is shalom, and everything he says after it unknots the fear. He says nothing of Joseph's trick; instead he gives the credit to their own God, and that line is the best piece of tact in the chapter. Rashi hears it as a tiered blessing: through your merit, or if not, through your father's. Rashbam notes that everyone in Egypt knew this family had a history of wonders. Whether he is a believer, a courtier repeating Joseph's script, or simply well-mannered, the text does not say.

The KJV 'I had your money' is brief and loosely worded; the Hebrew says 'your silver came to me', that is, the payment was received. A matmon is something hidden or buried, a treasure, not simply 'treasure': Ramban relates it to what is covered over. The debt is closed, and the 'treasure' is a gift. Ibn Ezra offers an everyday explanation, a forgotten hoard; Ramban a grain-market mix-up. The text leaves it a mystery.

Then, in a single clause, the release: 'he brought out Simeon to them'. Radak says he came directly from custody to reassure them. The moment of the chapter's first relief should be played as a quiet reveal: the brother they believed lost is walking toward them.

philological_notes.note: Hidden or buried wealth; from taman, 'to hide'. Radak: a blessing from God, like a man who finds treasure. Ramban stresses the sense of something covered.
'Your silver came to me': an accounting phrase, the payment arrived. The KJV 'I had your money' is a slightly different idiom.
'Peace', here wholeness and well-being, the greeting that releases fear.

verses.translation_literal: And the man brought [obj] the men [to] the house of Joseph, and he gave water, and they washed their feet, and he gave fodder to their donkeys.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then the man led them in, into the house of Joseph. He gave them water, and they washed the dust of the road from their feet. And he gave their donkeys fodder.
verses.directors_commentary:
Now the door is crossed. Rashi notes that this 'bringing' repeats 43:17 because they had been holding back at the entrance, and followed only after the word 'peace'. What follows is the standard ritual of hospitality: water for the feet, then care for the animals. Foot-washing was the first act owed a traveler in a land of sandals and dust; the same courtesy was offered to Abraham's visitors (18:4) and to Laban's guests.

The order is the host's: first guests, then beasts. Misp'o is fodder, the straw and mixed feed for donkeys. The KJV 'provender' is archaic and 'asses' is correct, though modern ears hear an insult in it. The verb 'gave' is used for both water and fodder: the same gesture of care for men and animals.

philological_notes.note: The customary welcome to travelers in sandals, after a day on dusty roads.
Fodder for animals: straw mixed with grain. KJV 'provender' is old English for the same.

events.title: The famine worsens and the grain runs out
events.narrative_summary: The famine is heavy in the land. When the family has eaten the grain brought from Egypt, Jacob tells his sons to go back and buy a little more food.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Anchored on the end of Jacob's refusal (Gen 42:38). The text says only 'when they had finished eating' (v. 2), with no length. I put 3.5 months, margin 1.2 months, so the earliest start is about 2.3 months (about 68 days) after the refusal. Floor: Judah says 'if we had not lingered, we would have returned twice' (v. 10), so two round trips of about 33 days each (about 15 days each way, urim travel Hebron-Egypt by donkey) fit inside the delay, about 66 days. Ceiling: Gen 45:6 (two years of famine so far when Joseph speaks), which the latest start (about 4.7 months) stays far below. MACRO_ERA: no time word marks the date.
events.ancient_season_marker: When they had finished eating the grain

events.title: Judah refuses to go without Benjamin and pledges himself
events.narrative_summary: Judah reminds Jacob that the man will not see them without their brother. Jacob blames them for mentioning Benjamin. Judah offers to be surety for the boy.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Continuous with Jacob's order (v. 2-3), so it starts when the previous scene ends. About an hour of talk, margin 1 day for when in the days after the grain ran out it took place. Judah's 'we would have returned twice' (v. 10) says the delay has been long.

events.title: Israel agrees and sends a gift and double silver
events.narrative_summary: Israel gives in. He tells his sons to take the land's best produce and double silver, with the returned silver, and he commends them to God Almighty.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Israel answers Judah at once (v. 11 'And Israel their father said'), so it follows the surety scene directly. A short speech; margin 1 day.

events.title: The brothers take Benjamin and go down to Egypt
events.narrative_summary: The men take the gift, double silver and Benjamin, and go down to Egypt.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Starts the morning after Jacob's consent (offset 1 day, SHACHAR departure), a day to gather the gift and silver. Hebron to Egypt by donkey is about 493 km, about 32 km/day, elapsed about 15 days (urim travel). The text gives no duration, so this is an estimate with a 2-day margin. DAY_SEQUENCE.

events.title: Joseph sees Benjamin and orders a midday meal
events.narrative_summary: The brothers stand before Joseph. He sees Benjamin and tells his steward to bring the men home, slaughter and prepare, because they will dine with him at noon. The steward does so.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Begins when the journey ends (dawn of the arrival day, about 06:00, as the journey was counted in whole days from dawn). The noon dinner ordered in v. 16 follows the same day, so a brief encounter and walk to the house lasts about 1 hour. Margin 3 days carries the journey's uncertainty.

events.title: The brothers fear for their silver and speak with the steward
events.narrative_summary: Afraid at being brought to Joseph's house, the brothers think it is because of the returned silver. They explain to the steward, who tells them not to fear and brings Simeon out to them.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Follows the walk to the house (v. 17-18) on the arrival morning before the noon meal. About an hour with a 1-hour margin. DAY_SEQUENCE: no hour is stated.

events.title: They are given water and prepare the gift
events.narrative_summary: The steward takes them in, gives water to wash their feet and fodder to their donkeys. They prepare the gift for Joseph's arrival at noon, having heard they will eat there.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Between the steward's talk and Joseph's noon arrival (v. 25 'against Joseph came at noon'). Taken as about 2 hours, ending before noon.

events.title: Joseph comes home; the brothers bow and he weeps
events.narrative_summary: Joseph comes home and the brothers give him the gift and bow to the ground. He asks about their father, sees Benjamin and blesses him, then hurries to his chamber and weeps.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Text says Joseph comes at noon (v. 25, 16). TZOHORAYIM is snapped from the start of the arrival event (about 06:00 on arrival day), so it is the same day's noon. About 30 minutes, margin 1 hour.

events.title: Joseph and his brothers eat; Benjamin gets five portions
events.narrative_summary: Joseph washes his face, composes himself and orders the meal. The Egyptians eat apart from the Hebrews. The brothers sit in birth order and Benjamin's portion is five times the others'. They drink and are merry.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Follows Joseph's weeping (v. 30-31) directly, so it starts when the reception ends, shortly after noon. A meal of about 3 hours, margin 1 hour.

causal_edges.causal_explanation: Joseph's secret return of their silver in the sacks (42:25) is why the brothers fear being brought to his house (43:18).
Seeing Benjamin with them leads Joseph to order a banquet for the men (43:16).
Hunger forces Jacob to send them back (43:2), and that makes Judah press the condition about Benjamin (43:3-5).
Having agreed and prepared the gift and the silver, the men take Benjamin and go (43:13, 15).
Judah's pledge to be surety for the boy persuades Jacob to say 'if it must be so' and send Benjamin (43:9-11).

entities.etymology_meaning: Hebrew minchah, a gift or tribute presented to a superior.
entities.summary_bio: A present chosen by Israel from the best products of the land: a little balm, honey, spice, myrrh, pistachios and almonds. The brothers carry it down to Egypt to win the favour of the ruler and present it to Joseph.
The residence of Joseph the vizier in Egypt, where the brothers are received, wash their feet and dine at noon. The text does not say in which Egyptian city it stood.

entities.etymology_meaning: Not a name: the Hebrew phrase means 'the one who is over his house'.
entities.summary_bio: The official who runs Joseph's household. He carries out Joseph's orders for the midday meal, calms the brothers about the silver in their sacks, credits it to God's provision, and brings Simeon out to them.

components.evidence_explanation: GEN.43.15: the men took the gift in hand and went down to Egypt.
GEN.43.26: they brought him the gift that was in their hand.
GEN.43.13: Israel tells his sons 'take your brother' and go back to the man.
GEN.43.18: the men were afraid because they were brought to Joseph's house, fearing seizure as slaves.
GEN.43.9: 'I will be surety for him; from my hand you shall require him.'
GEN.43.23: the steward brought Simeon out to them.

systems.name: Gift of homage
systems.ancient_near_east_context: Those seeking favour from a powerful official brought a minchah, a gift of valued local products, as a sign of respect and to open the way for a petition.
rules_and_mechanics: The gift is chosen from the best produce of the giver's land.
It is presented in person, with bowing.
It is meant to dispose the superior favourably toward the giver.

systems.name: Hospitality and the shared meal
systems.ancient_near_east_context: Receiving guests with water for the feet, fodder for the animals and a meal was the basic duty of a host across the ancient Near East; eating together sealed goodwill and set out rank.
rules_and_mechanics: A host provides water for guests to wash their feet and fodder for their animals.
Guests are seated by rank or age.
Portions of food show honour; a larger portion marks special favour.
Egyptians did not eat with Hebrews, so separate tables were set.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Joseph dines apart from his brothers and the Egyptians, seats the brothers by age, and sends Benjamin five times as much; they drink freely with him.
system_instances.significance_note: Benjamin, Rachel's other son, is singled out with five portions, and the brothers drink with Joseph; many readers see a test of their jealousy here, but the text states no purpose.

system_instances.outcome_summary: The brothers bow to the ground before Joseph, twice, and call their father his servant.
system_instances.significance_note: Echoes Joseph's dreams of Genesis 37 while the brothers still do not recognise him.

system_instances.outcome_summary: The steward gives the brothers water to wash their feet and fodder for their donkeys.
system_instances.significance_note: Ordinary hospitality eases their fear that they have been brought in as prisoners.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Israel has a gift of local produce and double silver prepared for the Egyptian ruler.
system_instances.significance_note: The father tries to secure the favour of 'the man' and to correct a possible oversight about the first silver.

system_instances.outcome_summary: The brothers bring the gift into the house and present it to Joseph.
system_instances.significance_note: They hand over Israel's tribute with bowing, as Joseph's early dreams foretold.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Judah offers himself as guarantor for Benjamin's safe return, accepting blame for ever if he fails.
system_instances.significance_note: This overcomes Israel's refusal and prepares Judah's self-offering in Genesis 44.

system_instances.outcome_summary: The steward brings Simeon out to his brothers.
system_instances.significance_note: The hostage of Genesis 42 is freed, a first sign that the ruler's intent is not harmful.

edges.description: The brothers bow to the ground before Joseph and present the gift.
Israel tells his sons to take gifts, double silver and Benjamin down to the man.
Israel asks God Almighty to give them compassion before the man.
Israel asks why they dealt so ill with him by telling the man they had another brother.
Joseph says 'God be gracious to you, my son' to Benjamin.
Joseph has Benjamin served five times the portion of the others.
Joseph tells his steward to bring the men home and prepare a meal for noon.
Judah makes himself answerable for Benjamin's safe return.
The steward brings Simeon out to his brothers.
The steward gives the brothers water for their feet and fodder for their donkeys.
The steward tells the brothers to fear not and says their God gave them the treasure in their sacks.
